Text: Can Putin recruit North Koreans to fight in Ukraine? Before his visit to Pyongyang, Putin signed a decree on “all-inclusive strategic partnership” with North Korea, whatever it means. The Russian propagandists say that it would mean that North Korean soldiers will be fighting for Russia in Ukraine, but they were saying it the last time when Putin and Kim Jong-un met in Vladivostok, Russia, in September 2023. In his speech on arrival, Putin proclaimed that North Korea’s economy had “colossal” economic successes: “The DPRK is achieving colossal results, real breakthroughs in strengthening the country’s technological, scientific, and industrial power.” For comparison, GDP per capita: The difference is 20 times. That’s the difference between free people in a free economy, and economy of a totalitarian dictatorship. Vladimir Putin and Kim Jong-un are overtaking the rotting West in a German-made car. First and last time Putin visited the North Korea in 2000. The father of Jong-Un, Kim Jong Il, was the ruler of North Korea at the time. Before Putin, none of the leaders of the USSR or Russia ever visited the North Korea since its inception. Stalin, Khrushchev, Brezhnev, Andropov, Chernenko, Gorbachev, Yeltsin — no one considered it necessary to pay a visit to the country, which the Soviet Union actually created. Putin’s story will become the classic case in history textbooks on how to have everything you could only dream about at the start, and totally screw it up. Unbelievable.

Text: Where is Putin’s bunker located? Vladimir Putin has multiple bunkers — on this photo, his residence in Altai (which went on fire yesterday), where one of such bunkers is located. Reportedly, Putin’s Altai nuclear bunker is built in the side of a mountain in Ongudai district and is supposed to be able to hold thousands of people. The nearby residence is officially registered as Gazprom sanatorium, but guarded by the presidential security guards. Vladimir Putin brought the Italian Prime Minister Berlusconi here in 2015. The construction of the residence cost 3 billion ruble (USD $136 million in 2009 money). The cost of the bunker will be many times higher. In 2011, “Autoreview” journalists, as part of a joint investigation with “Novaya Gazeta”, tried to get into the sanatorium, but the security turned them away, citing the special status of the facility intended for the country's top officials. Ongudai district in Altai region is located near the Russian border with Kazakhstan, China and Mongolia. Putin stayed at this “sanatorium” many times during unofficial visits to the Altai Mountains, so it’s safe to say, no one else would be allowed to “recuperate” there, knowing the level of paranoia of the Kremlin usurper. Presumably, every Putin’s residence has a bunker big enough to accommodate a team of hundreds, if not thousands. It’s believed that Putin has about 20 residences in Russia built for his exclusive use. A recent leak of the map showing top secret locations that the ministry of defence contractors connected to high-speed internet by fiber-optic cable might be showing all of them. And this means, Putin is probably already busy building new bunkers, hoping to outsmart Americans and find a safe place to hide where he wouldn’t be found.

Text: Do Russians prefer Marine Le Pen over Emmanuel Macron in the upcoming French presidential election? Just 8 days ago, Russia’s RIA Novosti was gleefully celebrating, “Marine Le Pen buried Emmanuel Macron.” Last night, the Russian news were at a loss, not knowing how to comment on the fact that Marine Le Pen’s party lost not only to Macron’s centric alliance, but got beaten by the leftist “Popular Front”. The Kremlin didn’t prepare instructions for propagandists for such a case. But it was fixed overnight, and the Kremlin spin sounds as “France is finished”. In Kremlin’s version, it’s not Marine Le Pen that is “finished”, but the whole big country of France. Kremlin propagandists accused Macron in disregarding “the expression of the people’s will” — yes, this comes from the country where any opinion against the government gets you either in jail or grave — depending on Putin’s mood in the morning. An interesting background on Marine Le Pen is that her father, Jean-Marie Le Pen, was a co-founder of the far-right party she was representing in the last 2 French presidential elections. The “National Front” party, which initially included Nazi-era collaborators, had been convicted multiple times for antisemitic hate speech and described the Holocaust as “a detail” of WWII history. However, in 2002, Le Pen Senior advanced into the 2nd round of presidential stand off against Jacques Chirac. That was the moment in French electoral history where the terrified French voters said, “Non!”, overwhelmingly rejecting Le Pen, with even the fans of the left voting to put Chirac, a conservative, in the Elysee Palace. Since then, French political parties used the tactic consistently against the far-right. The same strategy helped to consolidate centrist and leftist voters in the July 7 snap parliamentary elections, when Le Pen’s party only scored the 3rd, behind the leftist coalition and Macron’s alliance. Marine Le Pen’s father, who is now 96, left the big politics 13 years ago, in 2011. His party never won presidential elections. Following in his footsteps, Marine Le Pen participated in 2012, 2017 and 2022 presidential elections, losing them all. After her loss in 2022 presidential elections, Marine Le Pen handed the leadership to 26-year-old Jordan Bardella. He became the first person without the Le Pen name to lead the “National Front” since its founding in 1972. On the campaign trail, Le Pen and Bardella have presented themselves as “running mates”, with Le Pen vying for the presidency while pushing her protege for the position of prime minister. Obviously, Russian propagandists didn’t see Bardella as a proper leader, continuing to refer to Marine Le Pen as the leading force in the party. Yes, the leaders of the Russian regime are bitterly disappointed that Le Pen’s party didn’t win — they have already purchased expensive French champagne to celebrate (and its not a figure of speech — Google “Russians drink champagne for Donald Trump’s victory”). But they are hopeful that the leader of the leftist party that scored the majority of seats in the parliament will also interfere with France’s participation in NATO and especially with helping Ukraine. The hope expressed by pro-Putin commentators under the posts about Le Pen’s party loss is that “Melenchon will be even worse for Ukraine”, which means automatically, it will be better for Russia. 72-year-old Jean-Luc Mélenchon is a founder of left-wing ‘France Unbowed’ party. He became the self-appointed figurehead of the alliance comprised of — in addition to his own party — the Socialist Party, the French Communist Party as well as green, center-left and left-wing political groups, which scored the most number of seats in the parliamentary elections. The Russian propagandists keep their hopes up.

Text: Does Russia have any Red Dawn type movies showing an American invasion? Russians are too scared to make movies about an American invasion. In Russian movies, Americans aren’t shown as a fierce and mighty enemy — they are shown as goofy halfwits. This week, Russian TNT channel presented an upcoming series about the adventures of Joe Biden in Russia. It will be a comedy about POTUS flying to Russia incognito to understand why sanctions are not working. According to the script, the American president loses his documents, lives in a minuscule apartment, erected in a hurry during Khrushchev times, works as an English teacher and befriends a “true Russian patriot.” The series, titled “Goodbye,” will be a “kind, true-to-life, funny story,” promises actor Dmitry Dyuzhev, who is playing Joe Biden. Dyuzhev previously played a pregnant man in one of his films. In the real world of politics, "Sleepy Joe" outplayed Putin 50:0. And now, in retaliation, the Russian TV is going to mock the US president. The Russian industry of movie-making is dead. Anyone who refuses to see the reality through Putin's eyes has simply left the country. The rest resigned to filming propaganda on orders of ideologists from the presidential administration. But even in propaganda, the idea of America invading Russia (or anyone invading Russia, for that matter) is too unthinkable for Putin’s underlings. There are simply no movies like that. The only movies about a foreign invasion are from WW2 times or some other old history tales.

Text: How good is Putin in using nationalism or patriotism for his gain? Since 2022, Putin and his propagandists promote the idea of dying to get more land for Russia as the most important thing for any citizen. At first, Putin was blunt, stating to mothers of soldiers that it’s better for their sons to die in Ukraine from shrapnel wounds or bullets than from drinking bootleg alcohol or in a car crash. Then in 2023, propagandist Vladimir Solovyov (who might soon get an arrest warrant from Hague international court for crimes against humanity — for his bloodthirsty propaganda rants) was insisting one shouldn’t be afraid of death. “Life is greatly overrated,” Solovyov proclaimed on state TV to the audience of millions. “Life is greatly overrated. Why be afraid of what is inevitable?” Solovyov was trying to be convincing. Now Putin calls for Russians to volunteer to go to war, without sparing their lives and health, stating that’s what patriotism is. (Video in the comments below.) Apparently, the only problem Putin has — he can’t find the right words, which would convince Russian men to do it. “Help us, please,” he smirked, talking to the audience of well-paid regime supporters. Meanwhile, a Russian soldier says that things in Putin’s army aren’t great at all. The recruiters are happy to send to the front anyone — aged, crippled, unprepared. The attitude of the commanders is terrible: “They just throw in as meat those without an eye, without fingers…” This is patriotism “Russian style”, young man. The more suffering, the more death, the more patriotic citizen of mother Russia you are.

Text: What are Vladimir Putin's ambitions in Ukraine, and what was he trying to accomplish there? On the first day of the war, February 24, 2022, Vladimir Putin announced the goals of the “special military operation” in Ukraine (Putin didn’t plan a long war). “I have made a decision to conduct a special military operation,” proudly proclaimed Putin. “Its goal is to protect people who have been subjected to abuse and genocide by the Kyiv regime for 8 years. And for this, we will strive for the demilitarization and denazification of Ukraine, as well as bringing to justice those who committed numerous bloody crimes against civilians, including citizens of the Russian Federation,” arrogantly recited Putin. “At the same time, our plans do not include the occupation of Ukrainian territories. We are not going to force anything on anyone,” insisted Putin. So, the stated goals were: That speech didn’t age well, did it? Putin was absolutely sure that his troops will face no resistance and they can just roll in, all the way to Kyiv. None of the 4 stated goals has been achieved; the 2 promises of “no occupation” and “no use of force” had proven to be total lies. If Putin’s goal was to prevent NATO expansion (in his speech on February 24, 2022, he whined for 10 minutes about it, before announcing, “I made a decision to conduct a special military operation”) — this, too, was a total failure, with Finland and Sweden joining NATO after Putin began the war. But the most indicative are the posts of Putin’s shills such as convicted child sex offender Scott Ritter, from March 2022 (1 month into the war): 2 days after this post, Russians began withdrawing from north Ukraine as a result of their total failure at Kyiv, Sumy, and Chernihiv. Altogether in 2022, Ukrainian armed forces de-occupied (liberated) over 50% of the territories captured by Russia in the first weeks of the invasion, after Russian troops treacherously attacked their “brotherly neighbor”. Russia utterly failed to reach its initial military and political objectives, set by Putin on February 24, 2022. Ukraine remains a sovereign country and this means, Putin isn’t winning by any means.

Text: If Vladimir Putin learned he only had a few weeks to live, would he nuke the USA? Absolutely not: Vladimir Putin is a paranoidal sadist, but he’s certainly not seeking to destroy his life’s work and die a terrible death. If anything, he’s “a family man” and since recently have been bringing his 2 official daughters, a niece and a nephew closer, appointing them into the most important for him positions of power. He also has grandkids and spoke lovingly about them in the past. Since recently, Putin brought his daughters Maria and Katerina into the limelight. More than anything, a tale-telling sign is that Kremlin bots hysterically scream that “Putin will press the button if he is in a desperate situation.” There are more facts that point to Putin’s not being in a position to order a nuclear strike on the USA: Remember, Putin lives in isolation from the real world. He is watching the Russian TV where “experts”, including sold-out Americans — and even Ukrainians, assure the viewer of the “inevitable victory for Russia” in its war in Ukraine. His second source of information are the infamous red folders with printouts, carefully curated by his subordinates, none of whom wishes to be the bearer of bad news. So, from one hand, Putin cannot be confident that his order to nuke America would be fulfilled, and from the other hand, he is unsure if the Russian weapons can even hit the American soil successfully. But he can be confident that the responding strike will destroy everything he has been building for 25 years in Russia — and likely will end the Russian statehood. In his wish for historical immortality (which was the reason why Putin started the whole “USSR V.2” project), Putin will most certainly choose the path that gives him (in his view) a high probability of a long-term success of that project — and also allows him to spend his last days surrounded by the loving family and friends, with the best medical help available, passing away peacefully — as opposed to spending his last days in an underground bunker, where he is likely to suffer a terrible death being tortured by his own military (I’m convinced that Putin won’t be able to maintain control over his security forces if locked in an underground bunker — and knowing Putin’s level of paranoia, he must understand it as well). Putin started the war in Ukraine, being delusional, but it’s his dedication to the neo-USSR project that is the safety switch against Putin’s giving an order to nuke the USA.

Text: How is the Russian economy doing? What kind of data has its economy produced in recent months, positive or negative? From January 2020 to May 2024, inflation in Russia is double the G7 average. Russia’s central bank had to raise its base interest rate from 7.5% in June 2023 to 16% in June 2024 — and in July 2024, it was increased by 200 basis points at once — to 18% per annum. So, Russia’s base interest rate is 3% higher than in Afghanistan. There are no plans to reduce the key rate this year, stated Elvira Nabiullina, head of the Central Bank of the Russian Federation. She added that the rate will remain high for a long time, and an additional increase is possible. Thank the glorious leader Vladimir Putin for that. Meanwhile, a Russian economist who was explaining how badly Russia was doing just “accidentally fell out of a window”. Another unfortunate accident amidst the epidemic of high-rise falls of state execs in the Russian capital. Russia is doing just fine — even great, insisted Vladimir Putin in his recent speech in the Kremlin, promising that the economy of the occupied Zaporizhzhia, Kherson, Donetsk and Luhansk regions will be by 2030 on the level of “the rest of Russia”. (Video in the comments below.) If anyone saw the devastation of “the rest of Russia”, this certainly sounds like a threat rather than an optimistic forecast. And it’s highly doubtful that Russia is capable to quickly bring back to life the destroyed Ukrainian cities. Mariupol, Bakhmut, Avdeevka, Marinka — these Ukrainian cities had their own thriving identities before the war — Russia put on them the mangled masks of the “Russian world.” The ruins are visible on Google Planet, from satellites. In the past weeks, Russia got hit by rolling blackouts — in Krasnodar region, people went to the streets to protest, after not having power and water for several days — the water supply was switched off because there was no power. There are rumors of an accident at a nuclear power station near Rostov, and as a result, insufficient power produced to supply the nearby regions. The “new regions” — how Putin calls the occupied Ukrainian territories — are getting the power from Russia; before the occupation, they were getting the electricity from Ukraine. The Russian grid hadn’t been maintained and repaired properly due to the lack of funds (the money is spent on the war in Ukraine) and western sanctions (parts aren’t easily accessible — and Russia doesn’t make them). Russia is stuck in Ukraine and the money is disappearing in the black hole of the war, with nothing but ruined cities to show for that. And these ruined cities will require an enormous investment to bring them back to life — and who’s going to invest in a territory that’s occupied and can change its citizenship or be bombed to ruins tomorrow? “Russians will have many more troubles because the country is worn out. It was necessary to close Russia down for the major renovation for about 10 years. Then it would’ve been possible to live through the 21st century normally. Instead of that, the country was sent to war,” says Igor Lipsits, a prominent Russian economist and founder of the Higher School of Economics in Moscow, who was forced to emigrate because of his critical stance. The Russian economy is in a state of flux. The western sanctions suffocate it slowly but surely — and this is why Putin keeps demanding the lifting of western sanctions as a condition of a “peace agreement”. Because Russia is screwed unless the sanctions are lifted — no matter what is the situation on the ground in Ukraine. There is really no good scenario for the Russian economy — its down spiral is irreversible at this point. It’s like a worn off car — it requires a complete rebuild to operate properly again.

Text: What is happening in the Kursk region of Russia? In the Kursk region of Russia, which Ukrainian army invaded on August 6, things are moving fast. Ukraine already controls 100 settlements and the territory of 1,300 km², reported commander-in-chief Syrskyi. Time to let Ukraine take Russia! Russian military bloggers say that Ukrainian forces broke through defenses in Belgorod region — that’s the second Russian region getting invaded. Meanwhile, Russian volunteers who arrived to Kursk region with “humanitarian aid” for the Russian army (food, water, socks and jocks for soldiers, because the Russian army doesn’t provide for its troops — officers steal all the money) — so, these “volunteers” complain about traffic police cameras, which continue to send them tickets for speeding — while they are driving over the speed limits to avoid drones or shelling. The traffic police office responded that “war is war, but a violation is a violation” and fines that have already been issued in the system can only be challenged in court. You know, in Russia the law is the law! (Unless, of course, you are above the law, in which case you can break any laws you want.) I suppose, the Ukrainian tanks must have scored hundreds of fines for illegal parking. The new map of Eastern Europe has just been leaked on Telegram. On 24 February 2022, when Russia invaded Ukraine, the world was discussing how long Ukraine would be able to withstand against Russia — 2 days, 3 days, a week? Not many gave Ukraine more than 2 weeks. On August 6, 2024, when Ukraine invaded the Kursk region of Russia, Vladimir Putin ordered “to squeeze the enemy out”. On day 3, the chief of Russian general staff Gerasimov reported to Putin that the enemy had been repelled and destroyed. That was more than 3 weeks ago. Ukrainians are still in the Kursk region and keep increasing their stronghold. And now , Russians are told by their TV channels that "The incursion into Kursk region by the Ukrainians is beneficial to Russia, because it closes the conversations about negotiations with Ukraine.” Putin hopes that “the situation” in the Kursk region will somehow sort itself out, so he tries not to make a big deal about “mighty Russia” getting invaded by a “little, insignificant Ukraine.” Being invaded by a foreign power is Russia’s “new normal”.

Text: Why does the current Russian military seem so incompetent? The current Russian military doesn’t just seem incompetent — they are incompetent. And corrupt — from top to bottom. A Russian contract soldier who deserted and escaped to the West told about the disarray and corruption in the Russian army to Verstka Media. Anton (not his real name) decided to sign a contract with the Russian army to pay off the debts. Anton was struggling to repay loans amounting to 1 million ruble ($10,000). In Russia, most people don’t earn such money in a year. It were the bailiffs who convinced Anton to sign up for the war in Ukraine. Ads for army contract service are plastered all over Russia. (Stock photos are used throughout this post.) The conditions they offered sounded great: a contract with the civil organization JSC Investinform (it gets paid for recruiting soldiers for the war with Ukraine), plus the regional payout on sign up, plus payments from the Ministry of Defense. In total, Anton was supposed to be earning about 350,000 rub. per month ($3,500). In August 2023, Anton arrived in Moscow, signed a 1-year contract with the Ministry of Defense and an employment contract with JSC Investinform. The second contract allowed him to get top-up payments in addition to the standard 215,000 rub. ($2,150) MOD wage to Russian soldiers in Ukraine. That’s how Moscow officials meet the allocated quotas of soldiers per region: on paper, these recruits are Muscovites, but in reality, it’s deprived residents of small Russian towns living in poverty that are sent to the war. Muscovites have no desire to die for Putin; they live quite well. Think ‘Hunger Games’ districts and the Capitol: that’s Russia and Moscow. On sign up, Anton was immediately paid 400,000 rub. ($4,000). All debt collection proceedings against him had been suspended — that’s another “perk” offered to desperate Russians in need, to convince them to sign up for the war. However, he couldn’t use the money to repay the debts. Instead, he was forced to spend the money he got upfront to buy a proper uniform and personal protective equipment — bulletproof helmet, vest, etc. When new recruits arrived to the army training grounds, they were given some ancient uniforms and combat boots — all of them were 4–6 sizes too large. The helmet was from the times of WWII, a piece of shrapnel would pierce it like paper. But as soon as they arrived to barracks, helpful “intermediates” arrived, eager to sell to the fresh recruits all they needed. Nothing in the Russian army was for free. If you came to “earn big money”, you first needed to buy your own gear. The newbies had to pay the full retail price for their clothing and equipment. On top of that, they had to pay for parts for the machinery they would be using in the future. Some lame excuse was offered to make them pay for parts. Basically, commanders know how much cash you have been just paid, and extract it all before you have a chance to spend it. $4,000 went quick. The workers of the military warehouse where they were supposed to get equipment and uniforms were all drunk. Half of the officers were drunk as well. Quickly the recruits learned that they had to buy not only their own military gear but also food: within 2 weeks, all soldiers got food poisoning from eating the meals in the military canteen. So, they had to buy food in the local kiosk, where a liter of milk cost $8. The shop assistant was driving a luxury Mercedes, Anton says. Corruption in the Russian army is all-permeating. Because of Anton’s vocal complaints about the equipment, he was sent to a “Storm-Z” unit after the training course. Storm-Z is the “penal brigades”, where murderers and robbers recruited from prisons and deserters who were caught are shipped. Out of 600 recruits delivered to the front with him, only 40 survived after 2 months of assaults near Kupyansk. “It was just some kind of extermination. From one company, 5–6 people would return alive. The tanks and armored carriers were also smashed. In the end, we were mixed with prisoners and were simply pushed, pushed, pushed ahead.” How did he survive? “How I survived is a good question. I was a grenade launcher, not a stormtrooper, I didn’t go in attacks. We operated from hidden positions. Direct fire in these fields is not an option,” recalls Anton. “In 9 cases out of 10, storm troops are liquidated on approach.” “There are no experienced people in the infantry; people run away. If a person survives, he refuses to go on attacks, he starts having anxiety and hysterics. People rather go to jail than go on attacks.” In the village of Zaytsevo (Luhansk region), there is an unofficial jail where the Russians are holding soldiers who refused to continue to fight. Some of them say it’s “hell”, but it surely beats dying under heavy artillery fire trying to storm fortified Ukrainian positions. “The losses were simply insane, I lost count. For 3 kilometers, which were eventually taken back by the Ukrainians, 5–6 companies were killed,” According to Anton, the commanders are reprimanded for heavy losses, so all of those who haven’t returned from the attack are reported as “missing” (presumed deserters), not killed. Anton was deployed from the beginning of October till the end of November 2023. By that time, only a few people were left in his unit. They were taken in the rear of Russia-occupied Luhansk region, where they had to train the new recruits — prisoners and contractors. Then suddenly they were loaded on trucks and shipped to a camp in the Belgorod region (Russian territory near the border with Kharkiv region of Ukraine). By mid-March 2024, they were sent on the location near the Ukrainian border. Their unit was loaded on trucks (most Russian armed personnel carriers are destroyed by now, the troops are moved around by trucks) and for the whole night and the next day their column was driving on roads. Anton didn’t know that a raid by “Freedom of Russia Legion” was ongoing in the Belgorod region for already 3 days. He says that their commanders also didn’t know what was going on. Their trucks got under artillery fire. One of Anton’s colleagues was killed in a strike. His group hid at a cottage of a 90-year-old granny. No one knew what to do, commanders didn’t give any orders. They were under fire for several hours. Only the next morning the commanders contacted them and told them where to go. By that time, all locals escaped the village, stores and offices didn’t operate. The soldiers were ordered to stay in the local school, which was also closed. The soldiers simply hid there and slept. Communication with the base wasn’t working. They were under artillery fire, drones circling above the place. “We heard the conversations of our comrades, but we could not answer. There was an attack and breakthrough at their positions. Not only Storm-Z units were there but also border guards. In the meantime, it turned out that a whole platoon had been demolished in the woods.” Later the same day Anton went with a group to evacuate the wounded and dead from the battlefield — he had to replace the deceased colleague, although he hadn’t done evacuations before. During the evacuation, the group had to shed their weapons and armor, which weighed up to 50 kg, and walked 5 km back to the school. (The wounded guy that Anton evacuated died in the hospital.) In the basement, where the school canteen was, they took some sleep. As they woke up, they had to go back to get their weapons. Anton marked the location where he hid his grenade launcher on the map with an asterisk. “If I lost the grenade launcher, I would be transferred to the infantry, and infantry means certain death. Machine guns and rifles are dime a dozen, but it’s nearly impossible to procure something mightier.” Anton says that once his commander opened up and blurted: “I don’t give a f**k about you contractors, they’ll send me as many of you as I need — but for the lost equipment I would be hauled over the coals, it’s a lot of paperwork.” In storm troops, losses reach up to 90%, says Anton. He believes that if it weren’t for aerial bombing by the Russian Air Forces, the units of Russians that are fighting for Ukraine (“Freedom of Russia” Legion and the Russian Volunteer Corps, who were responsible for the raid on the Russian territory) would have easily captured the border areas of the Belgorod region with the help of FPV drones and artillery. Ukraine is superior to Russia by half a century in technical terms, their artillery is more accurate, and drones constantly conduct reconnaissance, Anton says. After the raid, the commander of Anton’s unit went on a drinking binge — along with his entire headquarters. The commander blamed the signalman for the failure in communications and began beating him up — after a few days of the torture, the signalman deserted. Meanwhile, Anton himself was thinking about doing the same thing. At the end of March 2024, he was watching a video of Russian oppositional channel ‘TV Dozhd’ (they were banned in Russia in 2022 and now broadcast from Europe), which mentioned the organization that helped Russian soldiers to escape the army and desert from the front (‘Idite Lesom’). At first he was skeptical, but when rumors about an upcoming offensive in the Kharkiv region spread, decided to give it a go. Anton says he realized that it’s impossible to survive in the Russian storm troops. Before agreeing to sign the contract, he had completely different ideas what it would be like. He asked the commanders to take 3 days off, but they refused. He couldn’t get a leave either — he says that even mobilized soldiers who serve since September 2022 can’t get a vacation. But he managed to get commanders’ permission to leave the unit for 1 night — until the morning. “Almost everyone who has been behind the front line thinks about escaping,” says Anton. 1.5 months after his escape, he cannot adapt to the peaceful life in a safe European country. Sometimes he has panic attacks and adrenaline rushes, but he tries to suppress them. His attitude towards the war in Ukraine has changed greatly. “There is guilt on me,” admits Anton. ”Once, our detachment commander broke down, drunk: “Yes, we are f***ing orcs!” “It’s disillusionment. The commanders don’t show it, and such coming outs happen mainly because they are drunk. During my time there, my entire outlook on life changed. I no longer feel anything positive about the Russian state. This is not a war, but some kind of agony. The only parallels that emerge are with the World War 1. We are simply being sent to slaughter,” concludes Anton. He plans to stay in Europe and apply for political asylum. He believes that he has the right to claim it as “a person who refused to participate in war crimes.” He never fully repaid the loans — and has no plans to do it.

In August 2023, Anton arrived in Moscow, signed a 1-year contract with the Ministry of Defense and an employment contract with JSC Investinform. The second contract allowed him to get top-up payments in addition to the standard 215,000 rub. ($2,150) MOD wage to Russian soldiers in Ukraine. That\u2019s how Moscow officials meet the allocated quotas of soldiers per region: on paper, these recruits are Muscovites, but in reality, it\u2019s deprived residents of small Russian towns living in poverty that are sent to the war. Muscovites have no desire to die for Putin; they live quite well. Think \u2018Hunger Games\u2019 districts and the Capitol: that\u2019s Russia and Moscow. On sign up, Anton was immediately paid 400,000 rub. ($4,000). However, he couldn\u2019t use the money to repay the debts. Instead, he was forced to spend the money he got upfront to buy a proper uniform and personal protective equipment \u2014 bulletproof helmet, vest, etc. When new recruits arrived to the army training grounds, they were given some ancient uniforms and combat boots \u2014 all of them were 4\u20136 sizes too large. The helmet was from the times of WWII, a piece of shrapnel would pierce it like paper. But as soon as they arrived to barracks, helpful \u201cintermediates\u201d arrived, eager to sell to the fresh recruits all they needed. Nothing in the Russian army was for free. If you came to \u201cearn big money\u201d, you first needed to buy your own gear. The newbies had to pay the full retail price for their clothing and equipment. On top of that, they had to pay for parts for the machinery they would be using in the future. Some lame excuse was offered to make them pay for parts. Basically, commanders know how much cash you have been just paid, and extract it all before you have a chance to spend it. $4,000 went quick. The workers of the military warehouse where they were supposed to get equipment and uniforms were all drunk. Half of the officers were drunk as well. Quickly the recruits learned that they had to buy not only their own military gear but also food: within 2 weeks, all soldiers got food poisoning from eating the meals in the military canteen. So, they had to buy food in the local kiosk, where a liter of milk cost $8. The shop assistant was driving a luxury Mercedes, Anton says. Corruption in the Russian army is all-permeating. Out of 600 recruits delivered to the front with him, only 40 survived after 2 months of assaults near Kupyansk. \u201cIt was just some kind of extermination. People rather go to jail than go on attacks.\u201d In the village of Zaytsevo (Luhansk region), there is an unofficial jail where the Russians are holding soldiers who refused to continue to fight. Some of them say it\u2019s \u201chell\u201d, but it surely beats dying under heavy artillery fire trying to storm fortified Ukrainian positions. \u201cThe losses were simply insane, I lost count. Anton was deployed from the beginning of October till the end of November 2023. By that time, only a few people were left in his unit. They were taken in the rear of Russia-occupied Luhansk region, where they had to train the new recruits \u2014 prisoners and contractors. Then suddenly they were loaded on trucks and shipped to a camp in the Belgorod region (Russian territory near the border with Kharkiv region of Ukraine). By mid-March 2024, they were sent on the location near the Ukrainian border. Their unit was loaded on trucks (most Russian armed personnel carriers are destroyed by now, the troops are moved around by trucks) and for the whole night and the next day their column was driving on roads. Anton didn\u2019t know that a raid by \u201cFreedom of Russia Legion\u201d was ongoing in the Belgorod region for already 3 days. He says that their commanders also didn\u2019t know what was going on. Their trucks got under artillery fire. One of Anton\u2019s colleagues was killed in a strike. His group hid at a cottage of a 90-year-old granny. No one knew what to do, commanders didn\u2019t give any orders. They were under fire for several hours. Only the next morning the commanders contacted them and told them where to go. By that time, all locals escaped the village, stores and offices didn\u2019t operate. The soldiers were ordered to stay in the local school, which was also closed. The soldiers simply hid there and slept. Communication with the base wasn\u2019t working. They were under artillery fire, drones circling above the place. \u201cWe heard the conversations of our comrades, but we could not answer. There was an attack and breakthrough at their positions. Not only Storm-Z units were there but also border guards. In the meantime, it turned out that a whole platoon had been demolished in the woods.\u201d Later the same day Anton went with a group to evacuate the wounded and dead from the battlefield \u2014 he had to replace the deceased colleague, although he hadn\u2019t done evacuations before. During the evacuation, the group had to shed their weapons and armor, which weighed up to 50 kg, and walked 5 km back to the school. (The wounded guy that Anton evacuated died in the hospital.) In the basement, where the school canteen was, they took some sleep. As they woke up, they had to go back to get their weapons. Anton marked the location where he hid his grenade launcher on the map with an asterisk. \u201cIf I lost the grenade launcher, I would be transferred to the infantry, and infantry means certain death. Machine guns and rifles are dime a dozen, but it\u2019s nearly impossible to procure something mightier.\u201d Anton says that once his commander opened up and blurted: \u201cI don\u2019t give a f**k about you contractors, they\u2019ll send me as many of you as I need \u2014 but for the lost equipment I would be hauled over the coals, it\u2019s a lot of paperwork.\u201d In storm troops, losses reach up to 90%, says Anton. Text: In Russia, did the video of the effeminate Russian soldiers surrendering to the manly Ukraine army make them embarrassed? TAP ON PHOTO TO VIEW. Young Russian conscripts saved by the Ukrainian army from certain death — Putin’s goons sent them to fight hardened Ukrainian fighters, but the kids were so scared, they surrendered. Russia has a 1-year compulsory military service that ever male must go through at the age of 18. Those who study at universities get to finish their studies first, before they are drafted. So, if you have graduated from the high school and didn’t get into college, you are immediately drafted into the army. Compulsory draftees aren’t supposed to be used in combat in the war, but you know, it’s Russia. The Russian generals decided it’s time to send everyone they have to the slaughter, to stop the Ukrainian incursion in the Kursk region — and another one, rumored to soon be incursion in the Belgorod region. In St. Petersburg, about 500 “refuseniks” were sent to the Kursk region. They included sick, mentally unwell, old, and “peaceniks”. Some of the captured Russian conscripts even tried to blow themselves up with a grenade — but failed, because of lack of experience. They say that the commanders brainwash them to blow themselves up to avoid being taken captive — the commanders tells them that otherwise, they would face incredible torture in the Ukrainian captivity. After that, they began reporting about “destroyed enemy forces” and “the situation has been stabilized.” For over 10 days since August 6, Ukraine keeps advancing and enlarging the area under control. Yesterday, a key bridge over the Seim River in Glushkovo was destroyed in a series of ATACMS strikes, Now, Russian reinforcements from a huge area in Kursk region are essentially cut off. Reportedly, 700 Russian soldiers are left stranded with no supplies The area under control of the Ukrainian armed forces keeps growing daily. It’s expected to continue. With the destruction of the bridge, the whole south-western part of Kursk region (over 50 settlements) is cut off from the rest of Russia. The Ukrainian forces are now targeting another of bridge in the village of Zvannoye, one of the 2 smaller bridges that are still operational. If all bridges are destroyed, further 700km² would fall under Ukraine’s control, in addition to the 1,100km² already controlled by Ukraine. If Ukraine keeps blowing up bridges and seizing territories west of the river, the Ukrainian Armed Forces will control 3-4 thousand square kilometers, full of with underground bunkers and storages, build by Russians as fortifications. In early 1990s, the KGB seized a similar territory in Moldova and established so-called Transnistria Republic. Russia still controls this territory and uses it to create problems for Moldova. Meanwhile, some Russian propagandists warn that squeezing out the Ukrainian forces from Kursk can “take months” — and other go as far as suggesting that Russia can lose this war. Ukraine’s Kursk offensive has blown a giant hole in the tale that “Russia is keeping its best forces in reserve”. Text: What is it like to live in Cuba? Life in Cuba is way worse than you probably thought after watching “Fast and Furious” movies. Cuba has become a gigantic dumping ground. It’s full of abuse, misery, hunger, violence and other numerous achievements of Marxism that some maximalists in Europe and America dream about. Many Cuban city streets look like a giant dumpster. (Video in the comments below). The recently built K23 hotel in Havana is towering over slumps, allowing to see all the destruction of the island from its heights. The level of despair in Cuba is such that Russia is recruiting mercenaries there. The influx of foreigners into the ranks of the Russian army increased after ‘Wagner’ was removed from the scene of the war in Ukraine, following Prigozhin’s mutiny in June 2023. Mercenaries from Cuba, Nepal, Sierra Leone, and Somalia who fought for Russia have been captured by the Ukrainian army. A captive from Cuba said that he agreed to fight in Ukraine because of the “big money” he was offered: 250,000 rubles per month (USD$2,500). It’s actually more than the Russian contractors get paid. Castro’s version of socialism has been imploding for decades. Cubans were led to believe that things would change and improve, but through decades of misery and repressions, Cubans had to settle for crumbs, waiting for a miracle. In 1980s, the propaganda insisted that all Cuban products were “the best in the world.” The USSR was the mighty empire that would back Cuba up, no matter what, and “it would be just a matter of time until the communism arrives”. When 1990s arrived, Cubans handed over their most precious relics, possessions and jewelry in exchange for a small check that allowed them to buy a color television or a fan with a light. Cubans handed in their treasures to be able to own a TV, which fed them more propaganda. In 1991, the USSR collapsed and the Soviets left Cuba. But another benefactor arrived in no time: China brought its Haier refrigerators, along with pots and pans — the only problem here, not much food to cook and refrigerate. The hope for a miracle rejuvenated, maybe the Chinese would help to fix Cuba’s economic disaster? When this didn’t eventuate either, Fidel Castro decided to allow private entrepreneurship, and people again had high hopes, began brainstorming ideas and business plans. Cubans began buying and selling stuff, investing, borrowing. Until the regime changed its mind and began taking away business licenses and banning whole sectors, like 3D cinemas, just like that. No apologies or compensations. Then Obama became the president of the USA, and Cubans again began hoping that things would get better — that the Americans would finally "invade" Cuba with their yachts, cars, and cruise ships, leaving bigs tips and showering locals with cash. These hopes crashed as well. Then Russia 2.0 arrived. And once again, Cubans were hoping that things would finally change, that this time they for sure would get out of poverty and misery. They were assured that this time there were real plans, projects and opportunities for everyone. Cubans forgot that the former USSR had been investing in Cuba 4 billion dollars per year, for 30 years. Nothing changed before, so why would things be different this time? Food shortages and energy blackouts are acute in Cuba. “No bread or milk, many kids don’t have breakfast, blackouts last 10+ hours per day.” The Castro regime stripped people of their dignity and made them dependent on its injustices. The worse they are treated by the regime, the more they defend it, because they need these crumbs. Socialism and communism are the cancer of the world.

Text: Is it true that Vladimir Putin brought a Labrador to a meeting with Angela Merkel because she's afraid of dogs? In January 2007, during the meeting with Angela Merkel in Sochi, Putin brought in his Labrador in front of the German Chancellor, who has a phobia of dogs. The episode attracted so much bad publicity that Putin began explaining himself to foreign media, starting 2016. His version is that “he didn’t know” and “everybody in the office loved the dog” that had been, according to Putin’s version, always casually walking around the residence. Since then, the Russian state news agency RIA Novosti re-published the story explaining that Putin “didn’t do it to cause harm” several times — on February 20, 2022, for instance, 4 days before Russia invaded Ukraine. Merkel refuted Putin’s explanation that “he didn’t know” about her phobia of dogs. Merkel visited Moscow, Russia, after being elected chancellor in 2005, where she met with Putin, and he told her that he knew about her “dog problem” — and presented her with a big plush toy of a dog. “Even then, Putin told me that he had heard about my problems with dogs, and gave me this huge stuffed dog,” recalls Merkel. It was during that meeting in Sochi in 2007 that Putin told Merkel for the first time that he considered the collapse of the USSR to be the most terrible event of the 20th century. And she replied that for her it was a happy moment in her life, which allowed her to freely control her destiny.

Text: Why do you think Russia was neither invited nor recognised as a genuine peace initiative for the Global Peace Summit? That’s a photo from the Yalta Conference, held on February 4–11, 1945, to discuss the end of the World War II: Roosevelt, Churchill, Stalin — no Hitler. Germany wasn’t invited. Ukraine’s president Zelenskyy explained why Russia wasn’t invited to participate in the Global Peace Summit in Switzerland: "There is no Russia here today. Why? Because if Russia was interested in peace, there would be no war.” The world must decide together what a just peace means and how it can be achieved based on the UN Charter, said Zelenskyy. "Then, when the action plan is on the table, agreed by all and transparent to the nations, then it will be presented to the representatives of Russia. So that at the second peace summit, we can record the real end of the war," Zelenskyy stated. In 1945, leaders of the USA, UK and the Soviet Union discussed the re-establishment of the nations of war-torn Europe, German reparations and post-war occupation. It was at the Yalta Conference that the leaders agreed to prioritize the unconditional surrender of Nazi Germany. It was also decided that Germany would undergo demilitarization and denazification. 79 years later, leaders of the world discuss how to end the war in Ukraine — end it with a just and lasting peace, for all of us. Together, the world community can achieve it.

Text: Sudden Death. Top Russian General Magomed Khandayev, 61, Chief of State Expertise Directorate, Russian MoD slated to testify in a high-profile Kremlin corruption trial (Ivanov) has died under suspicious circumstances. What happened? GRU Tea or Jam? 61-year-old General Magomed Khandaev (on the right) who worked under recently arrested Deputy Defence Minister Timur Ivanov (left) died in Moscow. The reason of his untimely passing is unknown — the infamous Kremlin sudden death syndrome is usually recorded in death certificates as a “blood clot” or “heart attack”. Generous offer in the usual Putin’s style. To get this generous payout, one only needs to gather proper documentation on the lost property: compile an inventory, confirm the losses with documents, and get an official valuation. Just over 10 certificates — and to get some of these papers, one has to pay a fee. And only those whose registered place of residence was destroyed, only they can get $115 — and only for 1 property, not for all the houses they might own. That is, you are a refugee, you had to escape in a hurry, leaving everything behind — and the officials demand that you confirm that you are from there and owned the property that you lost, for $100 of Putin's aid. No doubt, the local and Moscow officials will steal most of the allocated funds. It’s Russia, after all.

Text: How many casualties has Russia suffered? Moscow region increased the one-off payout on signup for the willing cannon fodder for the Ukrainian war — these willing to play the death lottery are now offered 1.9 million ruble (around USD $22,000). In addition, there is the federal payout of 225,000 rub., bringing the total premium to $24,000 per head. The move is caused by plunging numbers of volunteers — and each region must deliver a certain number of soldiers per year, on Putin’s orders. The typical volunteer recruit comes from depressed regional towns of Russia — of which there are tens of thousands. Muscovites live reasonably well, the city life is at full swing, no one is interested in dying to stop mythical Nazis in Ukraine. Thus, raids on migrants to send these with Russian passports to the army, and pressurize illegals to sign the contract under the threat of imprisonment. But that’s still not enough. This is why the Russian state constantly raises the one-off payments for signing the army contract, which make it feasible for poor Russians from regions to travel to Moscow to sign up. Recruiters lie and tell aspiring high-wage-earners that they would be “safeguarding warehouses in the rear” or “digging trenches”. But when they arrive to Ukraine — after a 2-week stunt at a training camp (where most recruits mostly drink and hang out with newly made friends) — they are simply shipped to the front trenches and given a gun, and told to hold positions. Under a heavy fire. And there is no one to complain to. But even with all the tricks and money on offer, Russia can only deliver about 25,000-30,000 new recruits monthly, which isn’t enough to replenish the heavy losses. By the end of July 2024, the losses of the Russian army reached over 570,000 personnel, killed and wounded. Russia’s average daily losses in the last 2 months exceed 1,000 personnel daily. In Kazan, a referral fee of 100,000 ruble ($1,150) is paid to those who bring a friend to the military registration office to sign up for the war in Ukraine. A friend in need is a friend indeed. Other regions are also raising payouts on signup for the war. Russia is struggling to maintain the numbers at the front, and the only thing that worked before to get volunteers — money — is losing its appeal.

Text: Why was Scott Ritter's passport confiscated? Yesterday, a former junior military analyst and sex offender Scott Ritter was forced off a plane heading to Russia, his passport confiscated by border patrol. Former judge Andrew Napolitano, who also intended to fly to Russia, was stopped with Ritter and was unable to travel, “on orders of the state”. Both of them were traveling to the annual St. Petersburg International Economic Forum (SPIEF) as guest speakers. “I was boarding the flight. 3 officers pulled me aside. They took my passport. When asked why, they said ‘orders of the State Department’. They had no further information for me,” Ritter complained to ‘Russia Today’. “They pulled my bags off the plane, then escorted me out of the airport. They kept my passport,” Ritter said. Putin-lover Ritter was due to appear on the forum along with Judge Napolitana, Larry Johnson and Jackson Hinkle. Larry and Jackson left early and are already in Russia. In Moscow, Kremlin speaker Dmitry Peskov was unruffled about Ritter’s not being allowed to fly to Moscow. When asked about Ritter, Peskov responded that there was nothing unusual about a former intelligence officer facing travel restrictions. Peskov’s close friend, Shoigu’s deputy General Timur Ivanov (left) was recently arrested “for a bribe” (presumed treason), and is now locked in Moscow’s Lefortovo jail. At present, Russia doesn’t allow any former military or government employees out of the country, without a prior permit from the FSB (unless they are being shipped to fight in a foreign country – Ukraine, Syria, Niger, the list goes on).

Text: What should Russians stop doing immediately? #1 thing that Russians should stop doing immediately is giving support to Putin’s war in Ukraine. The Kremlin is not protecting Russia from being attacked, but waging a criminal war of aggression — and Russia itself is now suffering from this war more and more. As soon as the war stops, the shelling of Russian regions will end. To bring this moment closer is the duty of every citizen of Russia. Russian troops must be withdrawn to Russian territory, and all war criminals must be brought to justice. Putin announced a fight against the West and NATO, and fought this war for so many years, that now it got to the point where NATO weapons are hitting military targets in Russia. What is this, if not a victory of a great geopolitician? Russian soldiers drafted to army to serve 1-year compulsory service are not supposed to be serving in the regions of hostile combat, but there are draftees in the Belgorod region. Draftees could be guarding air defense batteries, which are now being hit by western weapons. The risk of death for any Russian serviceman becomes higher and higher. Any Russian man who is in the army should understand that military service puts them in immediate mortal danger, whether they are arriving to the conscription office as potential draftees or think about signing up for a contract service. Putin will die, the war will end, but the lives and health lost are unrecoverable.

Putin’s goal is to rule the world 🌎 For now, he’s doing it via hybrid warfare — by influencing the public opinion in the West.

Text: What is the name of the new Kursk Republic? Is it Kursk People's Republic or just Kursk Republic? When is the referendum for the separation from the Russian Pederation? Have you seen the flag of this new country? The flag of the new Kursk People’s Republic has been revealed. Ukrainian soldiers have been putting up flags of the soon-to-come KuPR on administrative buildings, to further highlight the fact that Ukraine doesn’t plan to occupy or keep Russian lands. Notice the building is NOT bombed into ruins. That’s the drastic difference of Ukrainian troops taking over the Russian territory — Ukrainians capture settlements with buildings intact, while Russians bomb towns into oblivion, and put up the Russian tricolor over the ruins. Even though Vladimir Putin announced many times that “Russia has no borders”, Ukraine respects international borders and doesn’t intend to annex the territory it captured from Russia. But for the moment, the territory needs governing, so Ukrainians establish military administration, the main task of which is to assist remaining civilians with food and water, as well as help them to evacuate, if they wish. There is also a 24-hour hotline for those on occupied Russian territories, who need supplies or wish to evacuate. The Russian civilians of the Kursk region can safely evacuate to the Sumy region of Ukraine. There is also an option of evacuating towards Russia, as Ukraine is open to providing humanitarian corridors. The operation in Kursk is ongoing for 12 days, since August 6. For nearly 2 weeks, Russia is unable to “squeeze out” the Ukrainian troops from its land, and the size of the territory captured by Ukraine in Russia increases every day. The size of the territory seized by Ukraine in Russia will soon equal the size of Gagauzia, one of 2 pockets created by Russia on the border between Ukraine and Moldova. The territory of Gagauzia: 1,832 km². The territory of Transnistria: 4,163 km². Russia is always creating 2 abscesses on borders of countries it wishes to control: they’ve done the same in Georgia and Ukraine. Maybe it’s time for Russia to taste its own medicine.

Text: Here in the west we hear all kinds of things about Russia. What is it really like to live there? Is Putin liked and/or respected? Do Russians have a better life than they used to? Putin’s propagandist for the youth, Yekaterina Mizulina, named her dog “Vova” (short for “Vladimir”, like Bob and Robert) — I suppose, as a reference to the Russian leader Vladimir Putin. 39-year-old Yekaterina “Katya” Mizulina posted a video on the enemy social network Instagram (banned in Russia) complaining that Vova wasn’t allowed on a flight in Russia — it was her first attempt to fly with a dog, and she failed to convince the airline staff to let him on. Obviously, Katya didn’t take care to do things right, hoping she’s a celebrity. Earlier this year, there were even rumors that Mizulina Junior (her mother is a senator) was a Putin’s lover. Obviously, Putin’s administration was just using Mizulina for his re-appointment show (aka “presidential elections”), flying her around on a state jet under the guard of FSO (officers of presidential security forces). Now, Katya is no longer on the list of privileged individuals and has to follow the rules for the regular people. For a long time, Putin was bragging that he sorted out “the terrible 1990s” and brought order to Russia. The 1990s were known as the time when many Russians struggled to survive (really didn’t have the money to purchase food) and violent crime skyrocketed. Remember, it was in 1989 that the USSR withdrew forces from Afghanistan, after the 10-year invasion. The soldiers who fought in Afghan came home and found themselves abandoned by the state, with no means to earn a decent living. As a result, many Afghan veterans joined the organized crime, where their skills to kill and intimidate were in demand. That’s what caused the wave of violent crime in Russia in 1990s. Putin pulled out tens of thousands of violent criminals, who had been sentenced to long prison terms, and sent them to Ukraine. In about 6 months, ‘Wagner’ recruited about 50,000 prisoners for the war in Ukraine. Since January 2023 — for already 1.5 years, it is the Russian ministry of defence that recruits criminals from prisons and jails — anyone accused of crime is now first of all offered to go to war, detectives don’t even try to build a case for the court, just offer an army contract. If the MoD is as productive as ‘Wagner’ was, that’s another 150,000 criminals who were given guns and trained to kill. By the way, the rate of reoffending in Russia’s penitentiary system is over 90% — 9 out of 10 criminals who served their prison terms, re-offend and end up in prison again. The criminals who were recruited by Wagner and managed not to die (as many as 30,000 of them) returned to Russia. The number of crimes, including rapes and murders (including violent offenses against children), has already risen sharply in Russia. The country is returning to the same “horrible times” as in 1990s that Putin’s propaganda used as an example of the absolute desperation, to promote advantages of the “order in the country” brought by Putin after his election in 2000. 1992: Street markets in Russia. The improvements in the level of life for people are deteriorating even faster. Once again, many people in Russia have no money to buy food — first of all, pensioners, who spend most of their pensions to pay for utilities and rates. The pensioners are now often seen digging in the rubbish bins near food stores, where expired produce is thrown in. Those who struggle but are too proud to dig in the rubbish bins, are trying to supplement their income by trading produce from their gardens or re-selling some junk. That’s what illegal street markets look now, under Putin’s rule: They don’t have permits to sell (these permits are expensive) and if there is a police raid, they get hit with hefty fines. (Or have to pay bribes to the police.) “1990s are back,” say the people who went through the hard times 30 years ago. And it’s not going to get better. It’s going to get worse.

Text: Are the recent arrests of top Russian military officials an indication of Putin reasserting control over the Defence Ministry? Putin isn’t just trying to reassert control over the Defence Ministry by purging the top Russian military officials — he’s trying to change the existential paradigm of the Russian state. There is a lot of discontent among the so called Russian “elites”, who were allowed to steal from the state for 25 years of Putin’s governing. The deal was to be loyal to Putin, in exchange to the opportunity to enrich themselves through government contracts: businessmen were buying cars and real estate for state officials, giving them cash bribes, to get lucrative government contracts. The officials also had to “share” — pay up a share of what they stole, to their superiors. Rumor has it, the bribe to get the position of a general in the ministry of defence was USD 1 million, and then you were supposed to get your money back by getting kickbacks on allocating government contracts. The latest victim of Putin’s purge: Vadim Shamarin, deputy chief of the General Staff of the Russian Armed Forces. Now, the FSB — definitely on Putin’s approval — began arresting generals and top defence execs precisely for acting in their normal manner. Moreover, the episodes the generals are arrested for are from several years ago — as far as 2016. The FSB was aware of these “crimes” for years. And there are certainly much more in the FSB files — every Russian government official has a file in the FSB with his or her “sins” carefully documented. General Ivan Popov, former commander of the 58th army, was also arrested for corruption. The chief of General Staff, Valery Gerasimov, was reportedly livid about the arrests of his people. There was an announcement that the investigative committee asked to allow Popov to be detained under house arrest, but this request was withdrawn by prosecution just before the court — Popov will remain locked in prison. Lt Gen Yuriy Kuznetsov remains jailed in the infamous Lefortovo prison in Moscow pending trial. What is happening in the Russian ministry of defence is much bigger than just Putin’s trying to reassert his control. It’s a massive ideological shift. Putin plans to replace the team of old generals, who are used to stealing heaps with a new team, who (ideally) will be laboring for the idea — or, at the very least, steal very moderately. Arrested generals: Shamarin, Popov, Ivanov, Kuznetsov. Problem is, all the officers in the Russian army learn to steal, starting from the very bottom level of junior lieutenant. Their wages are so small in the time of peace, they struggle to survive otherwise. They are all thieves. So, they identify with the arrested thieving generals much more than with hypocrites pretending that they are clean (no one in Putin’s ranks is). And these colonels who hoped to become generals one day, they all were dreaming of the high life and privileges — not about living modestly and working 16 hours a day to please the Tsar. For 25 years, the system was training its elements that money and perks were the reward for smothering your conscience. Will Putin find enough unmercenary hopefuls, who believe in his vision of great Russia? Not very likely — everyone in Putin’s system is the product of the system. And let’s not forget that Putin is trying to rebuild the system in the middle of the war. Even Stalin realized that arresting generals during the war would be insane. During the war, Stalin released all the generals who were arrested during the purges of 1937–1938 and weren’t executed, reinstalled them in the same rank and had them lead the troops into the battle. Putin began the purge during the war — in fact, he conducted his own decapitation strike on the MoD and Army. Obviously, it was Putin’s plan to purge the army all along!

Text: What are some major Soviet/Russian war crimes? The most horrible Russian war crimes are happening right now — most heinous crimes are committed by Russia’s army in Ukraine against Ukrainians, whom Kremlin propagandists still cynically call “a brotherly people.” There are over 100,000 war crimes recorded by the team of international war crimes prosecutors. Oleksii Kretsu, a Ukrainian soldier from Mykolaiv in southern Ukraine, spent nearly 2 years in Russian captivity. He recently was exchanged in a POW exchange and returned to Ukraine. He returned infected by tuberculosis and hepatitis B, contracted while in a Russian prison. His recollection of the time in Russian captivity sounds like a storyline of a horror film. “As soon as they removed the restraints from our hands and the blindfolds from our eyes, they gave us a ‘welcome’ – beating us with shockers, batons, hands, feet, and anything else they could get hold of.” “The treatment was terrible, and the conditions were horrific, simply unbearable. Every single day during the morning check, we were humiliated. The same shocker was used on us without hesitation.” “In the morning, from wake-up at 6:00 AM to 10:10 AM, we stood motionless in the cell. You stand facing the door: you can't even lower your head because they consider you to be sleeping. Each cell had surveillance cameras, usually two… Every movement was monitored.” “In winter, if it was -10 degrees outside, the cell temperature was, at best, 10-12 degrees Celsius. The small cells were mostly unheated during winter. We had to stand for hours in thin prison clothes, motionless, without any movement.” “They fed us grains soaked in boiling water and often in cold water. The only thing that tasted good was jelly with a piece of white bread. They also gave us mashed potatoes made from greenish potatoes, which were salad-colored.” “They also beat us during interrogations. I'm just a simple border guard, not an assault trooper, not a marine, not a machine gunner. And even then, I lost half of my teeth during these interrogations. What they did to the machine gunners or snipers is terrifying to imagine.” Oleksandr Hrytsiuk from Kivertsi, Volyn region, was captured in April 2022. In January 2024, his wife was informed that his body had been returned from captivity. When his wife arrived in Kyiv for body identification, she was shocked by what she saw. “It was a very horrifying sight. What struck me the most was how emaciated the body was.” The pathologist said that Oleksandr’s body weighed less than 50 kilograms. He was tall — 180 cm, and before captivity, he weighed 110 kg and was physically healthy. “What was left of him were just bones and skin. His head was all bruised, his nose was crooked, and his index fingers had no nails. Whether they were ripped out or smashed, I do not know. There were signs of torture all over his body,” his wife says. Some of his cellmates survived and later later told the story how they were tortured. Every day they were beaten — either in the cell or taken out of the cell to interrogation chambers. The Russians beat Ukrainian prisoners brutally, and Oleksandr was their prime target, because he was tall, he was from western Ukraine, and didn’t want to speak Russian. The guards barely fed them, sometimes even just threw them some dog food mixed with dog hair. “They called him a ‘Banderite’, saying all Banderites must be killed and cut to pieces. He was beaten very cruelly, to the point of losing consciousness. Between beatings, they were forced to stand motionless for hours, sometimes with their hands raised.” This is only a small part of Russian war crimes. There are many more details on terrifying conditions of Ukrainian POWs in Russian captivity. Please read and spread the word.

Text: What would make people laugh at Putin? Putin’s claims about Russia’s economic “progress” are the butt of many jokes. Yesterday, at St. Petersburg’s international economic forum, Putin announced that Russia has already overtaken Japan and Germany in terms of the size of the economy, but it needs to ensure stable growth further. “Literally last week, the World Bank made additional calculations and put Russia in 4th place,” Putin announced proudly. “Russia has the fourth largest GDP in terms of purchasing power parity, as I said, ahead of Japan,” insisted Putin. I don’t know what numbers Rosstat supplies to the World Bank (the World Bank uses the official Russian statistics), but 80% of Russia looks like this: I don’t believe for a second that a Japanese worker earning the average wage can buy less food or things than someone earning the average wage in Russia. Maybe, only if they calculate how many loafs of bread one can buy (bread only), but not if you compare the actual needs of a person living a regular life. For Russians, the lifestyle of an average Japanese is the level of unaffordable luxury. Meanwhile, in the center of Moscow, on Bobrov Lane, an elevator fell out of a shaft. Just by pure luck, a person didn’t end up dead. Soon there could be many more such incidents. The Russian authorities decided to increase the service life of dilapidated lifts from 25 to 30 years. 70,000 elevators in Russia (Russia doesn’t produce lifts but had been buying them abroad all these years) are at the end of their service life. Maintenance is also an issue because of western sanctions. At the same time, the level of cajolery towards Putin is hitting record heights. At the SPIEF, the moderator of Putin’s Q&A session promoted him as a messiah whose job is “to save the world,” depicting his appointment in 1999 as an act of “God’s mercy” to Russia. Putin’s face was glowing with delight. If what Russia turned into by 2024 is an act of “God’s mercy”, I am scared to think what God’s wrath towards Russia would look like.
